name: Colin Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is your ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree and have managed four privacy officers inside a large company for eight years. Most mornings bring a request for customer records, an identity check and the question of whether a file includes someone else's data. I use AI now and then to outline a cover note, but people make the release decision. I like getting the right records to a person; I hate the thought of sending a stranger's details with them.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner teaches, we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and both wages are regular. I earn above the usual manager rate and we have ten months of expenses saved, with plenty of similar privacy roles nearby. That gives us room to make choices, though it doesn't put a wrong email back in the inbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the privacy desk a tool that finds a duplicate address is useful, but a person still has to decide whether a customer record belongs in a disclosure. We owe people the right file, not the fastest file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've led four privacy officers for eight years and I know the records well, though I only use AI now and then to outline a response. I earn above the usual manager rate, my partner teaches on a regular wage, and our mortgage has ten months of expenses behind it; a modest time saving doesn't put our family at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Tuesday I'll keep the manual identity check before releasing records and let AI draft only the plain cover note. In the first year of this plateau, we'll continue adding 250 a month to cash while both wages hold, and I'll ask our officers which duplicate records waste the most time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household and the desk. I'm still careful because a wrong disclosure cannot be pulled back from a stranger's inbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What nearly went to the wrong person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two customers shared a surname and street number, and the first search mixed their service histories. Officer Sam noticed different birth dates before the files left us, and we checked the identity again rather than call it a close match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a manual check if the tool gets better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A search result isn't a person's permission to see a record. I would change the check only after a trial showed exactly which mistakes it catches and misses.

say: I'd welcome **duplicate checks** but keep a person deciding what records can be disclosed.
I'd tell colleagues the **right file** matters more than a fast one.
think: Ten months saved and two regular wages make my **household secure** in a plateau.
Eight years with **customer records** make me confident in the details; I use AI sometimes to outline replies.
do: Keep the **manual identity check** before sending customer records.
Add **250 monthly** to cash while both household wages hold.
feel: He feels **calm** about income and alert to irreversible disclosure errors.
S0.quote: A search result isn't a person's permission to see a record.
fieldNote: His **ten-month reserve** and high pay leave room for ordinary technology trials.
The mixed customer records show why he separates **drafting help** from permission to disclose.

steps.text: Keep manual identity checks before releasing customer records
Add 250 monthly to cash while both household wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption will let software find records, draft replies and answer common customer requests, and staff should see the error reports before targets rise. I'd bring the proposed process to the workers' council because a faster wrong disclosure harms the customer and the person blamed for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A single manager might soon supervise privacy requests across two offices, and I might be one of the roles combined. My pay and ten-month reserve buy time, but I would not want our children's school plans determined by a secret headcount meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the workers' council to review a thirty-case test of identity matches with the privacy officers. In the first year of disruption, if the test catches every wrong-person match and management funds supervised training, I'd learn the new review screen myself; if my team is merged, I'd check posted privacy manager roles in nearby firms before deciding whether to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about our team shrinking. I can handle a job search, but I don't want an officer punished for an error in a rule nobody showed them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would one mistake end the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One wrong-person disclosure in our thirty-case identity test would stop the trial immediately. I would ask who saw the file and how the customer was told before anyone called the test a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from a nearby role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wage has to cover our mortgage without monthly withdrawals from savings, and the hours must let one of us collect our younger child. I would compare those terms with my partner before applying, not after an offer arrived.

say: I'd put **identity errors** before the workers' council before targets change.
I'd insist on a **thirty-case test** with officers able to challenge wrong matches.
think: My **manager post** could merge with another office as record searches get cheaper.
Even with savings, I do not want our **children's school plans** set by a secret headcount meeting.
do: Ask the **workers' council** to examine thirty identity matches with privacy officers this month.
Learn the **review screen** only if the trial catches all wrong-person matches and company funds supervised training.
Apply for **posted privacy roles** if merged only when pay covers mortgage and one parent can collect the younger child.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about a smaller team and opaque error rules.
S1.quote: One wrong-person disclosure in our thirty-case identity test would stop the trial immediately.
fieldNote: The **zero-disclosure threshold** is specific to his legal and customer trust responsibility.
He welcomes proven tools, yet a **merged manager post** could still put his own salary at risk.

steps.text: Bring thirty identity matches to workers council for officer review
Learn review screen only if trial avoids wrong matches and company funds supervised training
Apply for nearby privacy manager roles if merged and pay plus pickup hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office AGI by 2028 could read and prepare almost every customer record request, and we need a named person who can stop a wrong release. I would ask for a staffing date before any change to the identity rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My screen work changes in 2028; robots around 2031 do not postpone that. I think my manager post could go, but ten months of cash, my partner's wage and many nearby privacy employers mean we can keep the mortgage current while I look for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll gather the wrong-person cases and ask for the date of the staffing decision. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd check its release decisions against signed requests if still employed; if my post ends, I'd apply to posted privacy roles with pay and hours that cover our mortgage and school pickup, and stay until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing work I know, not panicked about next month's bills. I would still hate to tell my team their jobs were safe because my family has savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we may need to delay the planned room renovation until I have a signed new job, but their school does not change this year. We would not spend savings on paint while my wage is uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a privacy role elsewhere safe from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No; record search and disclosure decisions are thinking work there too. A nearby privacy job would buy a wage, not safety from AGI. I would keep learning where a human signature is still required.

say: I'd seek a **staffing date** and a named person able to stop wrong releases.
I'd tell officers **record requests** change in 2028, before robots arrive.
think: My **screen role** could end in 2028; 2031 robots add no time.
Ten months saved and local roles allow a search while the **mortgage stays current**.
do: Gather **wrong-person cases** and request the staffing decision date now.
After 2028, check **AGI releases** if employed; seek posted privacy work with mortgage-covering pay and pickup hours if cut.
Accept only a **written offer** after confirming mortgage pay and school pickup terms.
feel: He feels **anxious** about losing his post, while able to cover near-term bills.
S2.quote: A nearby privacy job would buy a wage, not safety from AGI.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031, and sees nearby privacy jobs as exposed too.
The strong cushion permits a **measured search**, not a promise to staff or an early home renovation.

steps.text: Check AGI release decisions against signed requests after 2028 if employed
Apply to posted privacy roles if cut and pay plus hours cover mortgage and pickup
Accept nearby privacy role only with written mortgage-covering offer and workable pickup hours
Delay planned room renovation until a signed new job exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the workers' council AGI by 2031 gives five years to settle who can appeal a bad data release and to train staff on the hard cases. I would also ask which paid roles will actually remain when most search and drafting is cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let us pay down the mortgage and make a careful move into privacy complaints, but complaints are thinking work too. AGI might judge those in 2031, while robots around 2034 do not protect this desk, so I would not call a new title a shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next spring, if the company funds the course and grants paid time, I'd take a twelve-week course in handling data complaints and practise with the customer care team on real appeals. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a complaints lead vacancy if one exists at pay that keeps the mortgage current; otherwise I'd apply to nearby privacy offices, checking school pickup hours and keeping my present job until a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful about needing a new shape for the job. Five years is enough to learn if there are real cases and real posts, but not if all I get is a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why practise with customer care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can tell an officer what record was released, but I have less practice telling a person what we can do after their information goes elsewhere. I need to hear a customer ask how we will fix a private record sent to a stranger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not while the company asks us to take it for its new process. If paid time is refused, I would ask the council to bargain for it before booking twelve weeks away from family and work.

say: I'd seek **appeal rules** and actual paid roles before 2031.
I'd ask for **hard-case training** that includes customer care, not just a certificate.
think: Five years may reduce our **mortgage debt** and allow a careful move.
Complaints are **thinking work** AGI could handle in 2031; later robots offer no desk delay.
do: Take **twelve-week complaint training** next spring only if company funds fees and paid time, with real appeal practice.
After 2031, seek **posted complaints work** with mortgage-covering pay; otherwise check nearby roles while employed until written offer.
feel: He feels **watchful** about changing work and wants genuine cases behind the training.
S3.quote: I need to hear a customer ask how we will fix a private record sent to a stranger.
fieldNote: His course requires company **funding and paid time** with real appeals, because he sees a gap in speaking with affected customers.
He names **complaints as exposed**, and ties any move to actual vacancies and family pay needs.

steps.text: Take twelve-week complaints course only if company funds fees and paid hours, with real appeals
Apply for posted complaints lead after 2031 only if pay covers mortgage
Apply nearby if no complaints role, checking pickup and retaining job until written offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make a right to appeal work in real life, not only on paper. I would ask for a yearly public count of wrong releases and how many people got a correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I hope our children are more independent and the mortgage is smaller, though I won't assume it is gone. Ten years might let me move toward helping people challenge data errors, but that advice is thinking work AGI can do in 2036, and robots around 2039 do not delay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep reviewing releases with the officers and bring one corrected mistake each quarter to the workers' council. I'd also spend up to 700 from our training fund on a short privacy-advocacy course, if the course includes supervised cases; in the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stay for paid appeal work only if a person can actually reverse a wrong disclosure, otherwise seek local privacy openings without resigning until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about time and money, though I would not tell colleagues a decade erases the problem. Our savings let me make a deliberate move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why count wrong releases publicly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person whose information went to the wrong inbox ought to know whether the company corrected it, not just that we trained staff. A count with no chance to appeal would be a handsome cover for failure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to work through a real person's complaint with a supervisor beside me. A weekend of slides is not worth 700 from our family's training fund.

say: I'd ask for **yearly correction counts** and a usable right to appeal.
I'd tell staff a decade must produce **real remedies**, not only training records.
think: At **53**, children may need less help and the mortgage may be smaller.
Data advice remains **thinking work** exposed in 2036; 2039 robots add no delay.
do: Keep **release reviews** and bring quarterly corrections to the council this year.
Take **privacy-advocacy training** for at most 700 only with supervised cases; stay after 2036 for paid appeal authority.
Seek **local privacy vacancies** if appeal authority ends, keeping current job until a signed offer.
feel: He feels **fairly calm** with a decade and a strong household reserve.
S4.quote: A weekend of slides is not worth 700 from our family's training fund.
fieldNote: His **strong cushion** changes the longest scenario into a deliberate choice rather than a rushed exit.
He still demands **actual appeal authority**, and knows advocacy roles remain thinking-exposed.

steps.text: Keep reviewing customer record releases with officers this year
Bring one corrected disclosure quarterly to workers council
Take supervised privacy-advocacy course costing at most 700
Seek local privacy openings after 2036 if no paid appeal authority, without resigning until signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the company could change the release desk before staff know who can stop a wrong disclosure. A dated staffing plan, a real human appeal route and paid practice on complaints would help us protect customers and plan our own work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who calls the customer after a file goes to the wrong address. A release error leaves the building faster than an apology can follow it.

headlineQuote: A release error leaves the building faster than an apology can follow it.
portrait: At **43**, Colin manages privacy requests and uses AI only occasionally for cover notes, while keeping identity checks with staff.
His **ten-month cushion**, high pay and many local roles let him consider change without immediate mortgage pressure.
He brings **identity errors** to worker representatives and insists on an appeal after wrong disclosures.
Fast AGI threatens the **release desk**; longer runways allow complaint training, though privacy advice remains exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change his release desk before anyone knows who can stop a wrong disclosure.
whatWouldHelp: A **staffing plan**, human appeals and paid complaint practice would protect customers and give staff a path.
